evidence: This is the A-page requirement in the current plan and batch manifest. The current draft page and def-scientific-statistical-model-contract body were inspected. Its observation-record, units/index/time-origin, quantity-status and sampling-law fields give the context for interpreting a time-indexed observation process. The definition remains draft and no independent acceptance is claimed. This batch conditions its mathematical statements on the specified law and makes no empirical adequacy claim.
The required page is published. The exact current definitions of real random variables, pushforward laws, expectation, variance and covariance used by this batch were inspected in their item bodies.

The required page is published. The current one-sided stationary-process/canonical-shift definition and Birkhoff theorem were inspected in full. The Birkhoff supplier assumes AC and gives almost-sure and L1 convergence only for an integrable strictly stationary process; its constant-mean conclusion requires ergodicity.

The published definition specifies a process as random elements indexed by a set and a finite-dimensional distribution as the pushforward law of a coordinate tuple, including coordinate order. The new definition uses exactly that finite-dimensional-law convention for integer shifts.
The published definition makes a real random variable a measurable map into R with its Borel sigma-algebra. The new definition assumes each coordinate is such a real random variable.
The published law is the pushforward probability assigned to target events by their coordinate preimages. The strict-stationarity clause compares these joint pushforward laws.

The published expectation definition is the integral against the stated probability measure for integrable real variables. This fixes the expectation notation in the finite-second-moment and constant-mean clauses.
The published definition supplies variance for square-integrable variables and covariance for pairs on one probability space. The weak-stationarity definition uses those exact meanings.

The published one-sided definition specifies finite-dimensional shift invariance, canonical path law, left shift, and ergodicity relative to that path law. Integer-shift invariance of X restricts to this definition for Y_k=X_{k+1}.
The published definition requires every strictly invariant set to be null or conull for the invariant measure. The corollary assumes ergodicity only for the canonical one-sided path law.
The published axiom is explicitly assumed by the Birkhoff supplier. This corollary carries AC unchanged and adds no separate choice use.

The current published proof was inspected. For AC and an integrable strictly stationary real process it gives almost-sure and L1 convergence to the conditional-expectation limit; under ergodicity it identifies that limit as the process mean. The consumer restricts the Z-indexed process to Y_k=X_{k+1} and verifies the one-sided hypotheses.

The published definition gives expectation as the integral on the stated probability space for integrable variables. It supplies the expectation notation used for the sample mean and L2 consistency statement.
The published definition supplies variance for square-integrable variables and covariance for pairs on a common probability space, which are the quantities expanded in step 1.1.
The published corollary gives linearity of expectation for integrable real variables. Square-integrability on a probability space implies integrability here by the explicit inequality 2|X_t|≤1+X_t².

The current published proof was inspected. Its statement gives covariance symmetry and bilinearity on finite linear combinations of square-integrable random variables, which yields the finite double covariance sum in step 1.1.
The published finite-space definition assigns each of the four displayed outcomes weight 1/4 and computes event probabilities by finite sums.
The published definition treats each coordinate projection on the finite outcome space as a finite-valued real random variable.
The published finite expectation is the weighted sum; direct enumeration gives the coordinate, product and joint-event probabilities used in the example.
The published finite covariance is the expectation of the centered product. The example computes means first and then the three pair covariances.

The published definition requires mutual independence to factor every joint point probability. The event that all three coordinates equal 1 has probability 1/4, whereas the product of marginal probabilities is 1/8.
